In addition, appellant was directed to pay a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- each to the legal heirs of deceased girls, as compensation.

sentences.text: The admitted case of accused Ashwani Sharma (appellant herein) was that the road accident in which the victim girls died was caused by Ford Ikon Car No. DL-3CS-3127 that belonged to him and that was purchased by him on the same day i.e. on 28/03/2001.

He raised defence that alleged eye-witnesses were not present at the spot at the time of accident;
they were interested witnesses and were planted as eye-witnesses by police.
It was argued that there were too many material contradictions in testimonies of key prosecution witnesses to rely on them.

13. Were eye-witnesses, interested witnesses? :
13.(i) The argument that PW2 Deepak being uncle of the victim children and PW9 and PW10 being friends of PW2, all of them were interested witnesses, is not tenable.
It is settled law that a witness cannot be considered as an interested witness merely on being a near relative of the victim

. An interested witness must have some direct interest in having accused somehow convicted for some extraneous reason [Ref. Amit Vs. State of U.P. (2012) 4 SCC 107].
13.(ii) It is observed that PW2, PW9 and PW10 were not known to the appellant before the incident, leave alone the question of having enmity between them.

sentences.text: Whether the accident was a result of rash or negligent driving of appellant?
Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in Ravi Kapur Vs. State of Rajasthan (2012) 9 SCC 284 that - 12.Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in the light of facts and circumstances of a given case.

entities.text: Ravi Kapur Vs. State of Rajasthan (2012) 9 SCC 284
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
It must be examined in the light of attended circumstances.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.
Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to "rash and negligent driving" within the meaning of language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the Legislature in its wisdom has used the words "manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life".

The preliminary condition, thus, are that - (a) it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted.

13.'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinary regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.
Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one; it is rather a comparative term.
It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.

Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.
In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence.
14.The Court has to adopt another parameter i.e. 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.

The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrians happen to be children of tender years.

It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others.
15.The other principle that is pressed in aid by the courts in such cases is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.

This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident but cannot prove how the accident occurred.
The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record.

sentences.text: Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act.
The courts have also taken the concept of 'culpable rashness' and 'culpable negligence' into consideration in cases of road accidents.

'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).

'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.

This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct.
[Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988' (1st Edn., 2010].

17.(iii) It was argued by Ld. Counsel for appellant that Ld. Trial Court wrongly discarded the testimony of DW1 Ashwani Sharma as unworthy of credit, although, his deposition was indicative of cogent and probable defence to prosecution case.
17.(iv) Sure, appellant Ashwani Sharma deposed in his defence but the story he introduced was completely fictional and make- believe.
No employment record of said Anurag Sinha in office of accused/DW1 Ashwani Sharma was produced in Court, especially for period around the incident.
No office employee deposed in favour of the appellant.
In the absence of credible basis, it is safe to conclude that DW1 introduced a fictitious character in the name of Anurag Sinha in the incident to avoid culpability.
Anyhow, DW1 talked to his mother on mobile call around the time of incident and furnished call detail record Ex. DW1/A1 of his mobile calls.
Does it, on its own, show that DW1 / accused Ashwani Sharma could not be driving his car while talking to his mother on mobile phone?
The answer is no!
Secondly, nothing prevented DW1 from showing the mobile call made to Anurag Sinha on 29/03/2001 through call detail records, like he did in respect of mobile calls to his mother.
In cross-examination by Ld. APP, DW1 replied that he went alone to purchase the car on date of incident and himself drove it from showroom to his office.
The said Anurag Sinha never before drove his car.
He replied that Anurag Sinha used to have a motorcycle and he never saw Anurag Sinha driving a four- wheeler.

In reference to deposition of DW1, Ld. Trial Court rightly observed that a small time marketing employee of the accused could not have picked up keys of newly purchased car and drove it without permission of the accused.

It is especially when, admittedly,
there was no prior occasion of said Anurag Sinha driving car of the accused.
The version of DW1 was incredulous and rightly rejected by Ld. Trial Court.
The filing of complaint with Commissioner of Police regarding false implication and then failure to pursue it is also indicative of attempt of accused/appellant to create false defence.
18. Ld. Trial Court rightly observed that if defence version about Anurag Sinha was true, accused could have informed the police about it soon after the incident, that he did not do.

After the incident, police as well as relatives of victim girls and public persons had gathered at the spot, which was close to the office of accused, but he avoided to meet them which was a conduct indicative of guilty consciousness of the accused, rather than his innocence.
19. In conclusion, it is observed that the impugned judgment dated 27/07/2019 is well reasoned and is based on correct appreciation of facts and evidence.
The appellant was rightly convicted for offence U/s. 279/304A IPC.
There is no substance in appeal and, so far as it impugns the judgment of conviction, it stands dismissed.
The issue of sentence shall be considered on completion of due procedure.

6
It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.
Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to "rash and negligent driving" within the meaning of language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the Legislature in its wisdom has used the words "manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life".
The preliminary condition, thus, are that - (a) it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted.
13.'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinary regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.
Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one; it is rather a comparative term.
It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.
Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.
In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence.
14.The Court has to adopt another parameter i.e. 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.
The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrians happen to be children of tender years.
It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others.
This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident but cannot prove how the accident occurred.
The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record.
'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).
'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct.
[Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988' (1st Edn., 2010].
